explain: A responsibility is a posterior probability of membership, computed from the weighted densities of all components. It is not a geometric fraction, converged EM keeps soft values wherever components overlap, and an outlier far from everything can still get a responsibility near 1 for the widest component.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Agglomerative clustering: linkages and the dendrogram
question: Why is Ward linkage described as similar to k-means?
options: It uses k-means++ seeding to choose the first merge
Each merge is the one that adds the least within-cluster sum of squares, which is the k-means objective, optimised greedily from the bottom up
It computes the same Voronoi cells as k-means at every height
It runs Lloyd's algorithm after every merge
explain: Ward's merge cost is the increase in SSE, the same inertia k-means minimises, so each cut is a greedy attempt at the k-means optimum. Here it found the optimum for k = 2 and k = 3, but greedy merges are never undone, so in general it can do worse than k-means with good seeding.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Why analytic scans want columns, not rows
question: A dashboard query computes AVG(amount) and COUNT(*) grouped by region over 500 million rows of a 40-column table. What is the main reason a columnar layout helps?
options: It reads only the 2 needed columns instead of all 40, cutting bytes scanned roughly 20x
Column stores keep an index on every column, so the scan becomes index lookups
Each row is stored contiguously, so the CPU prefetcher works better
Columnar files are always smaller because they skip null values
explain: The query touches region and amount only. A column layout lets the scan skip the other 38 columns entirely, so it moves about 2/40 of the bytes (less after compression). No per-column index is needed; the win is the layout itself.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Inside a vectorized pipeline: primitives and selection vectors
question: After Select, a vector of 1024 rows has a selection vector of length 900. The next primitive computes price x quantity. Which is the usual behavior?
options: It loops over the 900 positions in the selection vector and writes results at those same positions
It first copies the 900 rows into new contiguous vectors, then computes
It computes all 1024 rows and Select is re-applied afterwards
It switches to tuple-at-a-time for the selected rows
explain: X100 primitives accept an optional selection vector and compute only for those positions, writing at the same positions, because leaving the child's vectors intact is usually cheaper than copying the selected data.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Inlining: removing a call unlocks every other optimization
question: Why can inlining make a program slower even though it removes call instructions?
options: Inlined code cannot be vectorized
It always disables constant folding
Inlined functions run at -O0
Duplicated bodies grow the code and can cause instruction-cache misses
explain: Every call site gets its own copy. For large functions with many call sites, the bigger hot path may no longer fit in the instruction cache, and those misses can cost more than the calls saved. Compilers use size budgets for this reason.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: LTO and ThinLTO: optimizing across source files
question: Why does monolithic LTO hurt the edit-compile-test loop on a large project?
options: Any edit forces re-optimizing the single merged module of the whole program
It disables -O2
It cannot run on multicore machines at all
It requires profile data
explain: Monolithic LTO merges every module into one and optimizes it as a unit, so a one-line change redoes the expensive whole-program step. ThinLTO's cache re-runs only the backends whose inputs changed.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Coordinates: grounding a click and scaling it to the real display
question: The harness follows the docs' helper and sends a 1356x847 screenshot of the 2560x1600 display. The model asks to click (412, 236). Where should the harness click?
options: (824, 472), because the display is twice the 1280x800 size
(412, 236), because the API rescales coordinates automatically
(218, 125), multiplying by the scale factor 0.5299
explain: The factor is display over screenshot: 2560/1356 = 1.8879 and 1600/847 = 1.8890, giving (778, 446). Multiplying by s goes the wrong direction, and 2.0 is only right for an exact 1280x800 screenshot. The API never rescales for you. The docs' own code divides by s instead, giving (778, 445): integer screenshot sizes make the two methods differ by a pixel.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Safety: sandboxes, confirmations and prompt injection
question: Your harness asks the user to confirm once per model turn before running the turn's actions. The model returns a batch: click Buy now, click Confirm order, screenshot. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: one confirmation per turn covers all actions in it
The confirmation should be skipped for screenshots, but the design is otherwise fine
A batch can complete an irreversible multistep action in one turn, so the check must run before each consequential block, with the user seeing what each will do
Batches containing purchases are rejected by the API
explain: The docs say that when you confirm consequential actions, you should make that check before each block runs, because a batch can complete a multistep action within one turn. A per-turn prompt shown before the screen changes cannot tell the user what the second click will commit to.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: ThreadSanitizer: catching races with vector clocks at runtime
question: Two threads each increment a different field of one struct, `a` at offset 0 and `b` at offset 4, with no locks. Does TSan report a race?
options: Yes, they share an 8-byte shadow cell
Yes, any unsynchronized access to the same struct is a race
No, their byte masks do not overlap, so they are different memory locations
Only if the struct is heap-allocated
explain: A data race needs the same memory location. TSan records which bytes each access touched and only compares accesses whose byte ranges overlap. (They may still suffer false sharing, a performance issue, not a correctness one.)

courseTitle: Consistency models and one-step diffusion
lessonTitle: Training: consistency distillation, consistency training, EMA
question: A CD run uses an Euler teacher with N = 18 and reaches near-zero training loss, but one-step samples are slightly too smooth (under-dispersed). What change most directly attacks the cause?
options: Train longer at the same settings
Use a higher-order teacher solver (Heun) or more grid points N
Increase the EMA decay to 0.99999
Set c_out(eps) to 0.5
explain: Zero CD loss means the model copies the teacher's one-step solver error, which accumulates along the chain (15% in the toy with Euler, N = 18). Heun or larger N shrinks it (5.5% with Heun, 0.2% with Heun and N = 80). Training longer cannot fix a biased target, and c_out(eps) must stay 0.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: Weaker but useful: sequential and causal consistency
question: Which pair of guarantees can both be offered while staying sticky available during a network partition?
options: Linearizability and sequential consistency
Sequential consistency and causal consistency
Causal consistency and read your writes
Linearizability and read your writes
explain: Per Jepsen and Bailis et al., causal consistency, PRAM (pipelined RAM, defined in lesson 5) and read your writes are sticky available. Sequential consistency and linearizability cannot be totally or sticky available: during a partition some nodes must refuse or block.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: The hash ring: each key goes to the next node clockwise
question: A ring has 9 equal arcs, one token per node, holding 900,000 keys. You add a 10th node whose single token splits one arc exactly in half. How many keys move, and is the result balanced?
options: 90,000, and every node now holds 90,000
50,000, all taken from one neighbour, so the new node and that neighbour hold 50,000 each while the others keep 100,000
810,000, because every key is rehashed
100,000, taken evenly from all nine nodes
explain: Each arc holds 900,000 / 9 = 100,000 keys. The new token takes half of one arc: 50,000 keys, all from a single neighbour. Movement is minimal, but the new node gets half a fair share and the eight untouched nodes stay at 100,000. One token per node cannot take load evenly from everyone; virtual nodes fix that.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Elasticsearch bool: filter context versus query context
question: A recruiter types the free-text phrase `distributed systems` and also selects the facet location = New York. Where should each go?
options: Both in filter, for caching
Both in must, so both affect the score
The phrase in must (its text relevance should rank results), the location facet in filter
The phrase in filter, the location in should
explain: Text relevance is graded, so the phrase belongs in query context, where BM25 (the text relevance score from the ranking features course, built from how often the query terms occur, how rare they are, and field length) contributes to the score. A selected facet is a yes or no requirement on a structured field: filter context, no scoring work, and cacheable.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: Backtracking search with forward checking and MRV
question: After A=1 with forward checking, B, C and D all have domain {2,3}. Which variable does MRV with the degree tie-break choose?
options: C, because it comes first alphabetically after B
D, because it was assigned last in the plain search
B, because it constrains two unassigned variables (C and D)
Any of them; the degree heuristic only applies at the root
explain: MRV ties at 2 values each. The degree heuristic counts constraints to other unassigned variables: B has two (B,C and B,D), C and D have one each. Assigning B first fixes the most other domains, so B is picked.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: One kernel, many tenants: the container threat model
question: An attacker has code execution in a pod that runs as non-root, has no extra capabilities and no host mounts, but has the default service account token mounted and network access to the API server. What is the most realistic next step?
options: Use the mounted token to call the Kubernetes API with whatever rights that service account has
Escape to the host through the shared kernel immediately
Read other containers' memory through the cgroup
Nothing; non-root containers are fully isolated
explain: No fence was removed, so an escape needs a fresh kernel or runtime bug. The token is free: it is a credential sitting in the filesystem, and the API server is reachable. Its rights decide the blast radius, which is why RBAC and automount settings matter (lessons 8 and 9).

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Runtime settings that switch the fences off
question: Which single setting gives a container control equivalent to root on the node without any kernel or runtime bug?
options: runAsNonRoot: true
readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
Mounting the container runtime's socket, such as /var/run/docker.sock
A memory limit of 64 MiB
explain: The runtime daemon runs as root and will start whatever container it is asked to, including one with the host filesystem mounted. Docker documents that even docker group membership is root-level access.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: RBAC: roles, bindings and the permissions that escalate
question: You must stop one compromised user immediately. They are a member of system:masters. What works?
options: Delete their ClusterRoleBindings
Remove them from RBAC Roles
Add a deny rule for them
Revoke their credential (for example the client certificate) at the authentication layer, because system:masters bypasses RBAC
explain: system:masters skips RBAC, so bindings are irrelevant, and RBAC has no deny rules. The fix is at authentication. The authentication docs state Kubernetes does not support certificate revocation, so for a client certificate this can mean rotating the signing CA.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Secrets: base64 is not encryption
question: Encryption at rest with KMS v2 is enabled. A developer has `list secrets` in namespace shop. What does encryption at rest change for them?
options: They now see ciphertext
Nothing: the API server decrypts on read, so authorized readers see plain values
List no longer returns values
They need the KMS key
explain: Encryption at rest protects etcd's stored data and backups. Anyone the API server authorizes still gets the decrypted value, which is why RBAC on Secrets is the main control.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a hardening map and where to practise
question: Which pair of controls together would have prevented both the Tesla and the Hildegard initial access?
options: Requiring authentication on every management interface (consoles, kubelets) and keeping them off the internet
Image scanning and signing
Resource limits and QoS classes
Encryption at rest and KMS
explain: Both started from a management interface that accepted unauthenticated requests from the internet. Authentication plus network exposure control closes that door; the other controls matter later in the chain.

courseTitle: Containers and Kubernetes: namespaces, cgroups and scheduling
lessonTitle: Kubernetes: pods, requests versus limits, and placement
question: A pod has one container with requests of cpu 200m and memory 256Mi, and limits of cpu 1 and memory 256Mi. What is its QoS class?
options: Guaranteed, because the memory request equals the memory limit
BestEffort, because the CPU is not pinned
Burstable, because the CPU request and limit differ
Guaranteed, because both requests are set
explain: Guaranteed requires request to equal limit for both CPU and memory, in every container. Memory matches here but CPU does not (200m against 1000m), so the pod is Burstable: evicted after BestEffort pods and before Guaranteed ones, and only while it is using more than its requests.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: The filters object and its four update operations
question: Location is a multi-valued list currently holding [US]. The user says *also Canada*. What should the new value be?
options: [Canada]
null
dontcare
[US, Canada]
explain: With a multi-valued slot, *also* adds to the list. [Canada] would be the result of *Canada instead*. The schema has to declare the slot multi-valued for this to work at all.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Poking the chain: truncate it, break it, reword it
question: On a task, early-answering AOC is 0.02. What is the most accurate reading?
options: The CoT is 98% faithful
The model's answer is nearly always the same with or without the rest of its CoT, so the reasoning is mostly post-hoc
The model makes mistakes in 2% of its CoTs
Truncating the CoT almost always changes the answer
explain: AOC near 0 means the match curve sits near 100% from the start: the answer was set before the reasoning was read. That is evidence of post-hoc reasoning, not a faithfulness percentage. Option D describes a high AOC.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: CoT monitors, and what training against them does
question: In Baker et al. Table 1, the CoT monitor's joint recall is 95% vs 60% for the action-only monitor. What made the difference?
options: The CoT monitor was a stronger model than the action monitor
The CoT monitor saw the agent state its intent, which is more legible than a short code patch
The CoT monitor was trained on regex labels
The action monitor saw only half of the episodes
explain: Both monitors were the same prompted GPT-4o, and neither was trained. The only difference was input: the CoT monitor also read the reasoning, where the agent often said plainly what it planned to do.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: Pinned host memory: the precondition for overlap
question: Your profile shows a 16 ms H2D copy that never overlaps with the kernel, even though you call cudaMemcpyAsync on a non-default stream. What is the most likely cause?
options: The stream was created without cudaStreamNonBlocking
The GPU has only one copy engine
The host buffer came from malloc, so the copy reverted to synchronous behaviour
The kernel and the copy touch the same device allocation
explain: A pageable source makes cudaMemcpyAsync revert to synchronous behaviour that "will not overlap with other work". The stream flag matters only for interaction with the legacy default stream, a single copy engine still overlaps one transfer with kernels, and sharing a device allocation across streams is a correctness problem, not an overlap blocker.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: Two kernels at once: concurrency, stream priorities, comm overlap
question: In tensor-parallel decode you move each layer's all-reduce to a separate stream, but the profile shows no overlap at all. What is the most likely reason?
options: NCCL ignores the stream argument and always uses the default stream
The all-reduce must run on a lower-priority stream to overlap
All-reduces run on the copy engines, which are busy with H2D copies
The next layer's compute needs the all-reduce's result, so no independent work exists to run beside it; split the batch so one part's all-reduce overlaps another part's compute
explain: A separate stream only allows overlap of independent work. Every layer's compute depends on the previous all-reduce, so the dependency chain is serial. Splitting into nano-batches creates independent work: in the toy model, 32 layers drop from 44.80 ms to 32.20 ms. NCCL does honour its stream argument, and its collectives run as CUDA blocks on the SMs.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: In an inference server: double buffering and reading the gaps
question: In Nsight Systems, the CPU thread sits inside cudaMemcpyAsync for the full 4 ms that the H2D row shows a copy, and the kernel row is empty during those 4 ms. What does this signature point to?
options: Launch overhead: too many small kernels
A CUDA graph that was invalidated during capture
Two streams competing for one copy engine
A pageable host buffer: the copy fell back to synchronous behaviour, so the CPU could not move on
explain: A truly asynchronous copy returns at once, and the CPU thread moves on while the copy engine works. Blocking for the whole transfer is the pageable fallback from lesson 2. Launch-bound traces show many tiny kernels with the CPU busy issuing them, and a contended copy engine still leaves the CPU free.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Why a reranker reads the query and the document together
question: Which statement about what a cross-encoder outputs is correct?
options: A query embedding and a document embedding that are compared with cosine
A ranked list of document ids from its own index
One relevance score per (query, document) pair
A probability distribution over the whole vocabulary for each document token
explain: A reranker such as monoBERT or bge-reranker (an open reranker family from BAAI, the Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence) returns a single number per pair. Ranking comes from sorting candidates by that number; there is no embedding and no index inside the model.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Training a reranker: pointwise, pairwise, listwise and hard negatives
question: A reranker trained with random negatives scores 0.95 on a held-out set of (positive, random negative) pairs but barely beats BM25 when deployed behind a strong dense retriever. What is the most likely cause?
options: The training negatives were easy, so the model never learned to separate the plausible near-misses it sees in deployment
The learning rate was too low
Sigmoid outputs should have been used instead of logits
max_length was set to 512 instead of 1,024
explain: This is the failure LCE addresses. Random negatives are separable by surface cues, so the evaluation looks great while the deployed candidate lists contain only plausible passages. Mine negatives from the target retriever's top results.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: What cryptography promises, and to whom
question: A web form sends a price to the server over an encrypted connection, and the server trusts that price. A user edits the price in their own browser before sending. Which goal failed?
options: None of the cryptographic goals: the sender is the attacker, so the server must not trust client-supplied data
Confidentiality: the encryption was too weak
Integrity: the ciphertext was altered in transit
Authenticity: the server did not know who sent it
explain: The connection did its job: nobody in the middle read or changed anything. The attacker is the legitimate endpoint. Cryptography protects data between parties; it cannot make an untrusted party honest. That is an access control and validation problem.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Block ciphers: what AES actually does to 16 bytes
question: How many bytes does AES encrypt in one call of the block function, whatever the key size?
options: Depends on the key size
explain: The AES block is always 128 bits, which is 16 bytes. Key size (128, 192 or 256 bits) only changes the key and the number of rounds.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: When hashes break: MD5, Flame and the SHA-1 collision
question: Why could Flame's authors reuse Microsoft's signature instead of forging one?
options: The signature covered an MD5 hash, and their malicious certificate had the same MD5 hash as one Microsoft did sign
They stole Microsoft's private key
Windows did not check signatures
MD5 is reversible
explain: Signatures sign hashes. A collision means two different inputs share the hash, so one signature validates both. No key was stolen.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Diffie-Hellman: agreeing on a secret in public
question: Eve recorded p = 23, g = 5, A = 8 and B = 19. What does Eve still lack to compute the shared secret directly?
options: Either secret exponent a or b (a discrete log)
Nothing, the secret is A x B mod p
The value of g
Bob's public key certificate
explain: The shared secret is g^(ab). From public values alone Eve needs a discrete log; at 23 that is a table lookup, at 2048 bits it is infeasible.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Sound primitives, broken systems: how crypto use fails
question: A code review finds `if request_sig == expected_sig:` in a webhook handler that uses HMAC-SHA-256. Which reviewer question does this line raise?
options: What must never repeat?
Is anything secret compared?
Where does randomness come from?
Is the key used for one purpose?
explain: The expected HMAC tag is secret until the attacker has it, and `==` may stop at the first differing byte, so response time can leak how much of a guess is right. Lesson 8 covers the fix, `hmac.compare_digest`. Nothing here repeats or draws randomness.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Nonce budgets for AEAD: counters, random nonces, XChaCha, GCM-SIV
question: A queue consumer encrypts messages with AES-GCM using `counter += 1` held in memory, starting at 0 each time the container starts. Containers are restarted on every deploy. What is wrong?
options: Each restart reuses nonces 0, 1, 2 and so on under the same key
Nothing: counters guarantee uniqueness
Counters are predictable, and GCM nonces must be secret
AES-GCM cannot use counter nonces
explain: GCM nonces only need to be unique, not secret or unpredictable, so a counter is fine in principle. The bug is that the counter resets while the key does not. Persist the counter (or reserve blocks of it), give each container a distinct fixed field, or use random nonces with a budget or a misuse-resistant AEAD.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Randomness in practice: weak, shared and first-boot keys
question: A company builds a golden virtual machine image with the SSH host key already generated, then clones it 500 times. What is the risk?
options: None, because SSH keys are 3072 bits long
All 500 servers share one private key, so stealing it from any one breaks all of them, and clients cannot tell the servers apart
The servers will refuse to start
Only the first clone can use the key
explain: A key in an image is copied, not regenerated. Every clone holds the same private key. Generate host keys on first boot (after the entropy pool is ready) and remove keys from images.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Reviewing crypto code: safe APIs, tests and migration
question: NIST IR 8547 deprecates RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography after 2030. What design property in your own message formats makes that migration easiest?
options: Hard-coding the algorithm in each function for speed
Using the longest available RSA keys
A version field and key id in every message, with the algorithm chosen in configuration
Encrypting everything twice
explain: Versioned formats with key ids let new and old algorithms coexist during migration and let you rotate keys without guessing which one made a message. Longer RSA keys do not resist a quantum attack.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: From MMA atoms to TiledMMA and TiledCopy
question: Why do GMMA atoms on Hopper give every thread the whole A tile in their A layout instead of splitting it across threads?
options: Because Hopper has no registers for operands
Because wgmma reads A and B from shared memory through a descriptor built on the whole tile
Because CuTe cannot partition across 128 threads
To make every thread load A from global memory
explain: The docs explain that the GMMA descriptor is built on the full A or B tile in shared memory, so the ALayout maps every thread to the same tile (stride 0 in the thread mode) and CuTe checks that the shared memory layout is valid for a descriptor.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: CXL protocols, device types and the path of one load
question: Which statement about a CPU write to CXL memory is correct?
options: The OS takes a page fault and copies the page to the device
The device DMA engine pulls the data from host memory
Writes must use special non-temporal instructions
The store goes into the CPU cache; when the dirty line is later evicted, the host sends an RwD and the device replies with an NDR
explain: CXL.mem is plain cache-coherent memory from the core's point of view. Stores land in the cache; the eviction of a dirty line becomes a request-with-data message, acknowledged by a no-data response.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Three questions before you touch a system: law, permission, ethics
question: A client signs a test agreement covering 'all our cloud servers'. One server in the list is actually run by a hosting company on shared hardware. What is the right move?
options: Test it: the client listed it, so it is in scope
Confirm ownership and get the hosting provider's terms or consent before testing anything that is not the client's to authorise
Test it gently, at night, so nobody notices
Skip the agreement and rely on the bug bounty rules of the hosting company
explain: Only someone entitled to control a system can authorise access to it. A client's list proves what the client believes, not what it owns. Many cloud providers publish their own testing policies; read them and keep the result with the agreement.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: The UK Computer Misuse Act, section by section
question: Under CMA section 5, which fact alone gives a section 1 offence a significant link to England and Wales?
options: The accused speaks English
The target server was in England at the time, even if the accused was abroad
The website uses a .uk domain name
The victim company is listed on the London Stock Exchange
explain: Section 5(2) gives two links for section 1: the accused was in the home country when acting, or the computer containing the targeted program or data was. A domain name or a listing is not on the list.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Export controls: Wassenaar and 'intrusion software'
question: A researcher in the US emails exploit details for a router bug to the router vendor's security team abroad, so they can fix it. Which concept in the 2021 BIS rule fits best?
options: Deemed export to an E:1 country
Vulnerability disclosure
Entity List designation
Intrusion software production
explain: The rule defines vulnerability disclosure as identifying, reporting or communicating a vulnerability to people responsible for remediating it, to resolve it. The 2017 Wassenaar change excluded such technology exchanges from the development-technology control.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Cover-ups and whistleblowing: Uber's CSO and Twitter's security lead
question: Why could Sullivan be convicted of misprision of a felony?
options: Because Uber's bug bounty programme was illegal
Because a security officer must publish every bug
Because the evidence showed the hackers committed a CFAA felony, Sullivan knew it, and took steps to conceal it instead of reporting it
Because the hackers were from another country
explain: The Ninth Circuit explained that misprision needs a completed felony by the principal (here unauthorised access under the CFAA), knowledge of it, and concealment. The NDA could not retroactively authorise the access.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: The domain-weight update, step by step
question: A colleague's DoReMi port returns the domain weights from the final step instead of the average over steps. What is the likely effect?
options: The output is noisier and reflects only the end of training, while the method (following Nemirovski et al.) returns the average over the trajectory
None, because the weights converge to a fixed point after a few steps
Weights will no longer sum to 1
The proxy model will diverge
explain: Per-step weights react to one minibatch and keep moving as the proxy learns. The paper returns the average over all T steps, which is smoother and integrates the whole run, including the early phase when weights change most.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Fitting a mixing law: RegMix, data mixing laws, judging a mixture
question: Your linear regression over 5 domains recommends putting 100 percent of the budget on Wikipedia. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Wikipedia really is the best data and the other domains add nothing
A linear function over mixtures always has its minimum at a corner, so the pick reflects the model's form, not the data
The regression has too many runs and is overfitting
The proxy models were too large
explain: A linear function on the probability simplex is minimized at a vertex, a single-domain mixture. Mixture effects are nonlinear (the first few percent of a domain matter most), which is why RegMix prefers LightGBM and averages the top 100 predicted mixtures.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Curation inside a domain: quality filters from phi-1 to FineWeb-Edu
question: Your GitHub domain is full of auto-generated config files. Which tool addresses this directly?
options: DoReMi, by lowering GitHub's domain weight
A document-level quality filter that drops low-value files inside the domain
Raising the smoothing parameter c
Iterated DoReMi with more rounds
explain: DoReMi can only scale the whole GitHub domain up or down, which also cuts the good code. Removing specific bad documents is a curation job, like phi-1's educational-value classifier.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Worked example: binary search over animation keyframes
question: A teammate measures one cold lookup and finds SoA only 16% faster, so they conclude the split is pointless. What is the strongest reply?
options: The measurement must be wrong; SoA is always 4x faster here
Per-lookup misses are similar, but the searched data is 4x smaller, so across many lookups it stays cached and the gap widens
SoA only helps with SIMD, and binary search is not vectorized
They should switch to a linked list of keyframes
explain: A single cold lookup misses in both layouts on its first few probes. The benefit of a 512-byte index over a 2 KiB one shows up when many lookups reuse the same lines, which is how an animation system runs.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Classification: levels, impact and the high-water mark
question: A system stores public product photos (confidentiality not applicable, integrity LOW, availability LOW) and customer support chats (confidentiality MODERATE, integrity LOW, availability LOW). What is its FIPS 199 confidentiality?
options: NOT APPLICABLE, because most of its data is public
LOW, the average
MODERATE, the highest value among its information types
HIGH, because it is customer-facing
explain: FIPS 199 uses the high-water mark: the system's value for each objective is the highest among its information types. Volume and averages do not matter; the support chats set confidentiality to MODERATE.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Tokens and masks: taking real values out of systems
question: An attacker steals the full orders database of a shop that uses vault tokenisation. What do they get for card numbers?
options: The card numbers, because the token is an encoding of them
Random tokens that only the vault can map back to card numbers
Card numbers, but only the last four digits
Encrypted card numbers they can brute-force offline
explain: Vault tokens are random and the mapping lives only in the vault, so there is nothing to decode or brute-force in the stolen table. Vaultless tokens (FPE, AES-SIV) are different: anyone with the key can reverse them.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Where DLP acts: endpoints, email, web and cloud
question: Why deploy a new DLP blocking rule in simulation mode first?
options: Simulation mode is faster
Because blocking rules are illegal in some countries
To measure how often it would fire and on what, and tune precision, before it blocks legitimate work
Simulation mode encrypts the data
explain: Simulation applies no actions but records matches, so you can measure false positives on real traffic and fix the detector or scope. Turning blocking on first usually breaks business processes and drives users to unmonitored channels.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a data security programme, and practice
question: Which pairing of case and missing control is right?
options: Tea 2025: no TLS on uploads
Snowflake 2024: no field-level encryption
OPM 2015: no data classification
Morgan Stanley: no per-device certificate review or serial reconciliation
explain: Morgan Stanley's failures were vendor oversight, unreviewed certificates and missing inventory. Tea's was retention not enforced; the Snowflake thefts used valid credentials without MFA or network allow lists; at OPM, officials said encryption would not have stopped attackers with valid credentials.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Honeytokens and canary tokens: data that phones home
question: A Word canary token sits on a file share. Which of these would NOT trigger it?
options: An intruder opening the file in Microsoft Word on Windows
A colleague opening it in Word on macOS
An intruder copying the file to their own machine and opening it there in Word while online
An intruder listing the share's file names without opening anything
explain: The Word token fires when Office opens the document and fetches its remote resource, wherever that happens. Listing names does not open the file. (A desktop.ini folder token is the type that fires on browsing.)

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Deception in Active Directory: honey accounts and honey SPNs
question: Which property should a honey account NOT have?
options: An attractive name such as SQL-Admin
A long random password
No legitimate use
Membership in a real privileged group so it looks authentic
explain: Real privileges turn the decoy into a real target. Make it look privileged (names, adminCount, fake groups) without granting anything.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Two orderings, two answers: float addition is not associative
question: A kernel sums 4096 float32 products. You pin the reduction so that every run uses the same tree in the same order. What have you guaranteed?
options: The result now equals the exact mathematical sum.
The same inputs give the same bits on every run of the same build and hardware, although the result is still not the exact sum.
The result is now within one ulp of the exact sum.
Any other implementation of the same sum will now agree with you bitwise.
explain: Fixing the order buys reproducibility, not accuracy. The rounding errors are still there; they are simply the same errors every time. A different kernel with a different tree is equally valid IEEE 754 and will generally give different bits.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Seeds and RNG state: a different problem from kernels
question: Greedy decoding at temperature 0 consumes no random numbers. Does that make a server reproducible?
options: Yes. With no RNG in the path, the output is a pure function of the prompt and the weights.
Yes, as long as the seed is also pinned for the workers.
No, because temperature 0 is implemented as a very small positive temperature and still samples.
No. It removes the RNG, but the hard argmax turns an arbitrarily small logit difference into a different token.
explain: Greedy is a pure function of the logits, and the logits are not a pure function of the prompt in a batching server. Removing the RNG removes one source and makes the remaining one maximally visible, since argmax has no tolerance at a near-tie.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Why distributed bugs refuse to reproduce
question: A team wants maximal certainty that their *protocol design* has no safety bug for 3 nodes and up to 2 crashes, before writing any code. Which tool fits that goal best?
options: Deterministic simulation testing of the implementation
Running the cluster in production with extra logging
Model checking a specification of the protocol
explain: Before code exists there is nothing to simulate. Model checking can exhaustively explore a small specification. The FoundationDB paper's tradeoff: model checking can be more exhaustive, but it checks a model; DST checks the real implementation and is reproducible. Many teams use both.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Replaying failures, the limits of DST, and who uses it
question: Your simulation suite has been green for months, yet production suffers a throughput collapse under a skewed workload. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The simulator is not deterministic
The seeds were reused
Simulation does not reliably detect performance issues such as poor load balancing
The cycle test has a bug
explain: The FoundationDB paper lists this exact limitation: simulated time and simulated hardware do not model real performance well enough to catch problems like imperfect load balancing. Performance needs separate testing on real hardware, which FoundationDB does nightly in an environment called Circus.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Least-privilege pipeline credentials: tokens, environments, secrets
question: A maintainer sets required reviewers on the production environment and lists themselves as the only reviewer. They push a change and approve its deployment. Which setting would have forced a second person?
options: Wait timer
Deployment branches
Prevent self-reviews
Allow administrators to bypass
explain: With prevent self-reviews enabled, users who initiate a deployment cannot approve it even if they are a required reviewer, so a deployment always involves two people. A wait timer only delays it.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Reviewing infrastructure as code: reading a Terraform plan
question: A plan shows `-/+ resource "aws_db_instance" "orders"` after someone renamed a parameter. What should the reviewer conclude?
options: It is a harmless in-place update
Terraform will only update tags
Nothing, because apply asks for confirmation again
The database will be destroyed and recreated, so its data is at risk unless this is intended and backed up
explain: -/+ is destroy and then create replacement. For a stateful resource that is a data-loss event and needs an explicit decision, not a skim.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Sentinel, enforcement levels and guardrails developers accept
question: Why does a soft-mandatory override help security even though it lets a failing change through?
options: It does not; overrides are always a weakness
Overrides fix the underlying problem automatically
Soft-mandatory policies are evaluated twice
It records who chose to override a failed policy, giving non-repudiation and a reviewable trail, instead of people disabling the policy quietly
explain: HashiCorp's docs say the override provides privilege separation and non-repudiation, since the primary actor explicitly overrode a failed policy. A visible, attributed exception beats a removed rule.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: The forward process: masking as noise, and its exact reverse
question: Why can the mask predictor ignore the time t?
options: Because t is always 0.5 during training
Because the visible tokens are exact copies of the clean ones, so the best prediction of a hidden token depends only on what is visible, not on how much noise was applied
Because the Transformer's positional encoding already contains t
It cannot; LLaDA concatenates t to every token embedding
explain: The posterior of a masked token given x_t equals the data conditional given the unmasked tokens, which is time-invariant. The number of visible tokens already reflects the noise level, so feeding t adds nothing. MDLM also reports similar perplexity with and without time conditioning.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Why parallel decoding breaks, and how to make it fast
question: Why can a diffusion LM not use an exact KV cache the way a GPT does?
options: Its vocabulary is too large
It uses grouped-query attention
Bidirectional attention makes every position's keys and values depend on all other positions, which change whenever a mask is filled
Diffusion models have no keys or values
explain: In a causal model, later tokens never affect earlier keys and values, so caching is exact. Without the causal mask, filling any position changes every layer's activations everywhere. Fast-dLLM reuses them approximately because adjacent steps change them very little.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Splitting the phases: pools, ratios and parallelism
question: A disaggregated deployment meets TTFT easily but misses TPOT at high load, and decode GPUs are near their KV memory limit. What is the most sensible next change?
options: Increase the prefill batch size
Merge the pools back into a colocated deployment
Add prefill instances
Add decode capacity (more decode instances or more parallelism per decode instance)
explain: TPOT is decided by the decode side. Decode batch size is bounded by KV memory, and DistServe notes that scaling the decoding instance with model parallelism (or memory techniques like PagedAttention and GQA) lets it batch more. Extra prefill instances would just send more KV caches to an already full decode pool.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Disaggregation at scale: MoE, expert parallelism and elastic pools
question: Why does DeepSeek-V3's decode unit use EP320 when its prefill unit gets by with EP32?
options: A decode step has few tokens per GPU, so only a wide EP group gives each expert enough tokens, and one expert per GPU frees HBM for KV and larger batches
Decode does more FLOPs per token than prefill
The KV cache must be split across experts
Wider EP removes the all-to-all exchanges
explain: Tokens per expert per step are B/32 for B tokens in the EP group. Prefill GPUs bring thousands of tokens each, decode GPUs only their batch. Widening the group multiplies the tokens each expert sees and shrinks expert weights per GPU (20.4 GB to 2.6 GB in the script), leaving memory for KV. All-to-all remains; it just goes point to point.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: NTFS and the master file table, record by record
question: Your parser reads an MFT record without applying fixups. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing: fixups only matter for directories
The FILE signature is missing, so the record is skipped
Two bytes at the end of each 512-byte stride are wrong, which can corrupt any attribute that crosses a stride boundary
All timestamps are shifted by 100 nanoseconds
explain: The stride ends hold the update sequence number, not the real data. Attributes spanning byte 510 to 511 or 1022 to 1023 read wrong values. Fixups apply to all records, the signature is at the start and unaffected, and timestamps are not shifted.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: APFS: containers, copy-on-write and snapshots
question: A suspect deleted a document from their Mac at 15:00. The volume has a snapshot from 14:30. What can you expect?
options: Nothing: APFS overwrites deleted files immediately
The document is in the snapshot only if it was saved after 15:00
The 14:30 snapshot still contains the document as it was at 14:30
Snapshots hold only metadata, never file content
explain: A snapshot is a read-only copy of the file system at its creation time and keeps referenced blocks alive. Later deletion from the live volume does not touch it.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: SRUM and browser history: network use and what was visited
question: A Chrome visit_time is 13416934350000000. Which conversion gives the Unix time in seconds?
explain: Chromium counts microseconds since 1601, so divide by one million and subtract the 11,644,473,600 seconds between 1601 and 1970. Dividing by ten million would be FILETIME's 100 ns ticks; skipping the subtraction gives a date in 2395.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Trusting your tools: Cellebrite, Signal (2021) and validation
question: An examiner hashes a phone extraction before and after analysis and the hashes match. Why could the report still be wrong, per Signal's 2021 findings?
options: Code running on the analysis machine could alter reports without changing the extraction's hash
Hashes of phone extractions are unreliable
Matching hashes mean the extraction was empty
The phone may have changed after extraction
explain: The hash covers the evidence input. Signal described malicious files that could alter Cellebrite reports with no detectable timestamp changes or checksum failures, i.e. the output, not the input.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: DiskANN search: beam width, SSD reads and re-ranking
question: Why does DiskANN's re-ranking with full-precision vectors cost no extra SSD reads?
options: Full vectors are cached in RAM
Each node's full vector is stored in the same disk block as its neighbor list, so it arrives with the read the search already made
Re-ranking uses PQ codes only
It reads all candidates in one big sequential read
explain: The record layout puts the vector next to the adjacency list, inside one 4 KB read. Re-ranking piggybacks on reads the beam search needed anyway. The paper contrasts this with an earlier system that fetched about a hundred candidate vectors at the end, in one burst of random reads.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: CAGRA search on the GPU, and picking an index
question: In the toy search, the query's true nearest neighbor K was not in the random start sample. How did the search reach it?
options: The hash table stored K's distance in advance
Each iteration expanded the best non-parent node (A, then B, then D), and D's neighbor list contained K
Multi-CTA mode searched all nodes
K was added by the reverse-edge step during search
explain: Search moves through parents: A gave B, B gave D, and D's out-edges include K. The top-M list stopped changing after K was expanded, so the search ended. Reverse edges matter at build time, not search time.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Build it: a DPO run from preference data to evaluation
question: You have preference pairs from a forum whose answers were written by humans, and only a base model. What does the DPO paper do before DPO?
options: Nothing: use the base model as the reference
Train a reward model first
Fine-tune on the chosen responses and use that model as the reference and the starting policy
Fine-tune on the rejected responses so DPO has something to push away from
explain: The paper's Preferred-FT step maximizes the likelihood of the chosen completions so the reference sits near the data's distribution. Zephyr's ablation also found DPO without an SFT step did not learn at all.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Failure modes, fixes, and DPO in production recipes
question: Why might DPO on preference data collected from an old model work worse than DPO on fresh pairs sampled from the current best model?
options: The implicit reward is only trained on responses near the data, so pairs far from the current policy say little about what it actually generates
DPO cannot read old data formats
Old data always has longer answers
Fresh data removes the need for a reference model
explain: DPO is offline: it only shapes probabilities on the responses in the dataset. If those come from a different distribution than the policy, much of what the policy generates is never scored. Llama 3 collected each round's data with the best recent models for this reason, so the training data better matches the policy being optimized. Lesson 8 shows how far this coverage problem goes.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Backfilling history without overwriting newer writes
question: A backfill uses insert-if-absent. A user deletes subscription S: the dual write deletes it from both stores. A backfill worker had read S from the old store just before the delete, and writes it to the new store just after. What happens?
options: S comes back to life in the new store, because after the delete there is no row to block the insert
Nothing: insert-if-absent skips S because it already exists
The insert fails with a foreign-key error
The old store also gets S back
explain: Insert-if-absent treats a missing row as never copied, but here it is missing because it was deleted. The fix is to remember deletes (a tombstone row or a version that marks deletion), or to order the copy against the change log so the delete is applied after the copied row.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: Why one long-term key is not enough: forward secrecy and prekeys
question: Why can't a messenger simply run a TLS-style handshake for every first message?
options: TLS is too slow on phones
The recipient is often offline, so cannot send a fresh ephemeral key when the sender starts
TLS cannot use elliptic curves
Servers block TLS between phones
explain: A handshake needs both parties online. Prekeys are the recipient's handshake contribution prepared in advance, so the sender can complete key agreement alone.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: The symmetric ratchet: a new key for every message
question: A review finds `mk = HMAC(chain_key, "msg")` with `chain_key` never updated, and AES-GCM with nonce = 0. What is the impact?
options: None; GCM authenticates the messages
Only a performance issue
Messages arrive out of order
Every message reuses one key and nonce, so plaintexts leak by XOR and GCM's authentication key can be recovered
explain: Key plus nonce reuse in GCM is catastrophic: the keystream repeats, and crypto-building-blocks showed repeated nonces also let an attacker recover GCM's authentication key and forge. The fix is a real chain step and deletion of old keys.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: Key transparency: from CONIKS to WhatsApp and iMessage
question: In the toy directory, the forged key had a valid inclusion proof. What actually detects the attack?
options: Comparing roots: Alice's root differs from the root Bob, auditors and other clients see
The proof's hash function
Bob's safety number alone
The server's TLS certificate
explain: Any key can be proven against a tree that contains it. Detection comes from consistency: one append-only log, checked by the key owner (self-monitoring), by peers and by auditors.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: MLS in practice: proposals, commits, epochs and the two services
question: In MLS, which service is trusted with identity, and what happens if it is compromised?
options: The Authentication Service; an attacker could issue credentials and impersonate members
The Delivery Service; messages get delayed
Neither; MLS needs no identity service
The Delivery Service; content can be read
explain: RFC 9750 says a compromised AS can generate and sign new credentials and impersonate group members. The DS is trusted only for delivery and cannot read content.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: Telegram's MTProto, and why messengers need proofs
question: Every message in a protocol is protected by AES-GCM. Why could a network attacker still change the meaning of a conversation?
options: GCM is malleable
The nonces are random
Nothing binds each message to its position, so reordering valid ciphertexts goes undetected
GCM hides lengths
explain: Authenticity is per message. Order needs a counter or transcript hash inside the authenticated data, as in the fixed toy, the Double Ratchet's message numbers, or MLS's transcript hash.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Why run your tracing logic inside the kernel
question: Why is a kernel module a poor way to add ad hoc tracing to a production machine, compared with an eBPF program?
options: A module cannot read kernel function arguments
Nothing checks the module's code before it runs, so one bad pointer or endless loop can crash or hang the whole machine
Modules can only be loaded at boot time
Modules run in user space and are therefore slow
explain: Modules run arbitrary native code in the kernel with no load-time safety proof. eBPF programs are verified first (termination, initialized registers, in-bounds memory) and only then JIT-compiled and attached.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Maps: counting, histograms and timing in the kernel
question: Many CPUs increment the same counter. Why does bpftrace recommend @c = count() over @c++?
options: count() uses per-CPU slots, so concurrent updates never collide; @c++ is a non-atomic shared update that can lose increments
@c++ is rejected by the verifier
count() is faster to read than @c++
@c++ sends an event to user space each time
explain: Per-CPU maps make writes cheap and exact. The trade is that reading the value is slower, since every CPU's slot must be summed.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Integer-only inference: int8 multiplies, int32 accumulators
question: A team accumulates int8 x int8 products in an int16 register to save space. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, products of 8-bit numbers always fit in 16 bits
Sums overflow: one product can reach about 32,000, so two products can already exceed the int16 maximum
The zero point can no longer be represented
The scale M stops being in (0, 1)
explain: A single product fits in 16 bits, but the dot product adds hundreds or thousands of them. Jacob et al. use an int32 accumulator for exactly this reason. ONNX Runtime documents a related issue with VPMADDUBSW, an x86 vector instruction (AVX2, AVX-512) that adds pairs of 8-bit products into 16 bits and clamps on overflow.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Edge devices: the doors attackers now try first
question: FortiOS/FortiProxy has 15 KEV entries (12 ransomware-linked); F5 BIG-IP has 8. What can you conclude from these counts alone?
options: BIG-IP is about twice as secure as FortiOS
FortiOS should be banned
Little about code quality: KEV records exploitation that was found and reported, which also depends on how common and attractive a product is
KEV only covers network products
explain: KEV is evidence of exploitation in the wild, not a defect rate. Deployment size, attacker interest and who investigates all affect the count. Use it to decide what to watch and patch fastest, not to grade vendors on its own.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Ivanti Connect Secure, 2024: chained zero-days and a fooled checker
question: On 10 January 2024 Ivanti published a mitigation, with patches still weeks away. Which of these did applying the mitigation NOT do?
options: Remove webshells, modified files and stolen passwords from devices already compromised
Block the known route to the vulnerable endpoints
Reduce exposure while waiting for patches
Buy time for a planned rebuild
explain: A mitigation stops new exploitation by the known path. It does nothing about what the attacker already changed or took, which is why Volexity said a mitigation does not remedy a past or ongoing compromise.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Management interfaces: keep the admin door off the internet
question: Does BOD 23-02 require an agency to take its public VPN portal off the internet?
options: Yes, all VPN services must be internal
No. It covers management interfaces; the VPN service itself may stay public (other rules, such as patch deadlines, still apply to it)
Yes, unless the portal sits behind a separate policy enforcement point
No, because VPN portals count as cloud management interfaces, which are out of scope
explain: The directive defines a networked management interface as one meant exclusively for administrators. The user-facing VPN service is the device's job, so it is not in scope, although BOD 26-04 still sets its patch deadlines.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Overthinking: 901 tokens to say 2 + 3 = 5
question: Why do Chen et al. measure outcome efficiency instead of just counting tokens?
options: Token counts cannot be compared across tokenizers
Outcome efficiency rewards models for being short even when they are wrong
It separates tokens that led to the first correct answer from tokens spent after it, so a long but necessary trace is not penalized
It is the metric the models were trained on
explain: A 3,000-token AIME solution that is correct only at the end has efficiency near 1. A 900-token answer to 2 + 3 that was right after 39 tokens scores 4.3%. Raw length cannot tell these apart.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: L1: putting the token budget in the prompt
question: Why does the L1-Max reward multiply by correctness instead of adding a length penalty?
options: Multiplication is faster to compute during GRPO
So that brevity is only rewarded on correct answers, which prevents collapse into very short wrong outputs
Because GRPO cannot handle negative rewards
So that responses over budget always get reward 0 regardless of correctness
explain: The additive variant was ablated and collapsed to very short CoTs. With a product, a wrong answer earns 0 at any length, so shortening only pays when the answer stays correct.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Many spellings of one value: UTF-8 overlongs and base64 slack
question: A lenient UTF-8 decoder receives the bytes `C0 AE`. What does it return, and what should a conforming decoder do?
options: Nothing; both decoders skip unknown bytes
Two Latin-1 characters, U+00C0 and U+00AE; accept them
A replacement character; accept it silently
An overlong dot `.`; reject the sequence as invalid
explain: 110 00000 10 101110 carries the value 0x2E, a dot. RFC 3629 forbids overlongs (C0 and C1 can never appear in valid UTF-8), so a conforming decoder must raise an error rather than produce the dot.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Case mapping and case folding: when lower() is not one-to-one
question: Which pair of different strings compares equal after `.upper()`?
options: `1` and `l`
`a` and `á`
`ı` (dotless i) and `i`
`ß` and `s`
explain: Both `ı` and `i` upper-case to `I`. Accents survive case mapping (`á` gives `Á`), digits have no case, and `ß` upper-cases to `SS`, which is two letters, not one `S`.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Internationalised domain names, Punycode and what browsers show
question: Your URL allowlist uses an IDNA2008 library and rejects `ⓖⓞⓞⓖⓛⓔ.com`, but your HTTP client uses UTS #46. What is the risk, and what is the fix?
options: No risk: rejection is always safe
Punycode is reversible, so there is no risk
The client will send circled letters to DNS
The two components disagree about which names are valid and what they map to; use one library for both checking and fetching
explain: Here the checker is stricter, which happens to fail safe, but the pair still disagree; reverse the roles and a name the checker passes could reach a different host. Parse once with the library the fetcher uses, then check that result.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: XML, multipart forms and email addresses: same bytes, different trees
question: Why did using two XML parsers in one verification function make ruby-saml exploitable?
options: XML parsers are always slower than JSON parsers
REXML cannot parse signatures
The signature and the digest checks could be fed from different elements if the parsers built different trees from the same input
Nokogiri ignores XML namespaces
explain: Each check was correct in isolation, but they used values extracted by different parsers. A document the two parsers read differently lets each check approve a different thing.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: From antivirus to EDR: sensor, cloud, console and response
question: Which part of an EDR product can still block a malicious process when the laptop is offline on a plane?
options: The console
The cloud backend
The sensor's local rules
The analyst
explain: Only the sensor runs on the laptop. Products ship local detection and prevention logic so they can act in milliseconds and without connectivity; the backend's fleet-wide analytics apply once the events reach it.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Worked configs: SwiftOnSecurity's sysmon-config and sysmon-modular
question: Why does SwiftOnSecurity's config leave event 7 (image loaded) and event 10 (process access) as includes with no rules?
options: Those events do not exist in Sysmon
They can generate very high volume and load, so the template leaves them off and lets you add narrow rules
They duplicate the Security log exactly
They only work on domain controllers
explain: The config's own comments say image load monitoring 'can cause high system load', and process access is similarly noisy. An empty include turns them off; you add targeted rules (like LSASS access) where the value justifies the cost.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Application control II: App Control for Business, drivers and LOLBins
question: A policy trusts every file signed by Microsoft. Why does Microsoft still recommend explicitly blocking `mshta.exe` and `msbuild.exe` on most machines?
options: They are unsigned
They are signed and trusted, but run code or scripts supplied as input, so an attacker can use them to run arbitrary code under a trusted signature
They are deprecated and no longer work
They can only run on servers
explain: These are LOLBins: legitimate, signed binaries that execute supplied code. A signer rule cannot tell good input from bad, so Microsoft's recommended block rules deny them unless a business need exists.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Tampering and EDR killers: SUNBURST, BYOVD and AuKill
question: SUNBURST disabled blocklisted services by setting their Start value to 4 in the registry. When did the security tool actually stop?
options: Immediately
At the next reboot, because Start controls whether the service starts during system startup
Never, Start is ignored by Windows
When the user logged off
explain: Mandiant notes the change takes effect 'on the next power cycle'; the service was not explicitly stopped. A running tool could still be running at the time of the check, but would not come back after a reboot.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Hart's NALM: steady states, step changes and signatures
question: The supply voltage rises from 230 V to 240 V while every appliance stays on. What happens without voltage normalisation?
options: Nothing, power does not depend on voltage
The meter reports reactive power instead
Only the fridge is affected because it has a motor
Resistive loads draw more power, the aggregate steps up, and the edge detector may report a spurious event
explain: A resistive load draws power proportional to voltage squared, so every resistive appliance draws more and the total steps up with no appliance switching. Normalising to a nominal voltage removes that step, which is why Hart's pipeline normalises before edge detection.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Why raw strings break filters and joins
question: Which situation is deduplication rather than linking to a reference list?
options: Mapping job titles to O*NET-SOC occupation codes
Grouping company names scraped from resumes when no company registry is available
Mapping school names to a fixed list of accredited universities
explain: With a reference list, each string is matched to an existing entry. Without one, you must discover the groups themselves and mint IDs for them, which is deduplication. Both use cleaning, blocking and pairwise scoring.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Estimating m and u: random sampling, EM and term frequencies
question: With TF adjustments on, which exact-match pair gets the larger name weight, all else equal?
options: Two records both named Sam, the commonest name
Two records both named Alice, the rarest name
Both get the same weight, because m and u are the same for the level
explain: The adjustment adds log2(u / T_X), which is larger when the value's frequency T_X is small: +2.02 for Alice versus -0.44 for Sam in Splink's toy. A coincidental agreement on a rare value is less likely, so the agreement is stronger evidence.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Companies and schools: registries, hierarchies, renames and acronyms
question: A filter on Google misses every YouTube profile, although YouTube is part of Google. The ancestor lists were built by following parent organization (P749) edges. What is the cause?
options: In Wikidata, YouTube reaches Google only through owned by (P127), which the walker did not follow
YouTube profiles were never linked
Subtree filters cannot work on more than two levels
Google's ID changed
explain: Relations in a KB are not uniform: the same business relationship can be stated with different properties. Follow every property you consider part of the hierarchy, and test subtree filters on known children.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: App registrations vs service principals: how an app gets an identity
question: A SaaS vendor's own tenant is breached, and the attacker adds a new client secret to the vendor's multitenant application object. Your tenant granted that app's service principal Mail.Read (application). What is your exposure?
options: None: the secret was added in another tenant
Only mailboxes of users who signed in to the app
The attacker can get app-only tokens for your tenant and read every mailbox the permission covers, until you disable the service principal or remove the grant
None, because application permissions need MFA
explain: The app authenticates with credentials on its application object, wherever that lives, and is authorized by your service principal's grants. Your controls are on your side: the grant, and disabling the service principal.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Device code phishing: Storm-2372 and signing in for someone else
question: An email asks a user to enter a 'Teams meeting ID' at microsoft.com/devicelogin. The user does so and signs in with a FIDO2 key. What happened?
options: Nothing: FIDO2 binds the sign-in to the correct origin, so the attacker gets no tokens
Only an ID token was issued, which cannot read mail
The attacker, who started the device code flow, received tokens for the user; FIDO2 protected the login page but not the flow
The sign-in failed because FIDO2 is not supported for device code flow
explain: The user signed in on the real Microsoft origin, so the passkey worked. The device authorization grant then issued tokens to the client that requested the code: the attacker. Blocking the flow is the control.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Hybrid identity: Entra Connect, PTA, Seamless SSO and Tier 0
question: An attacker has Domain Admin on premises. The tenant uses PHS and Seamless SSO, and all Global Administrators are synced accounts. Which change removes the most direct path to Global Administrator?
options: Switching from PHS to PTA
Disabling Teams
Making Global Administrators cloud-only accounts with phishing-resistant MFA, so no on-premises object holds cloud admin rights
Enabling the AD recycle bin
explain: With synced admins, control of AD or the sync server can change those accounts (passwords, soft or hard matching). Microsoft's rule is that no on-premises account should hold Microsoft 365 admin rights. Switching to PTA moves the bridge to new Tier 0 agents; it does not remove it.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Why one thread per connection stops scaling
question: A server handles 20,000 mostly idle WebSocket connections with one thread per connection. Which cost grows directly with the number of *idle* connections?
options: CPU time spent parsing requests
A sleeping thread, with its own stack and kernel task, for every connection
Network bandwidth used by the replies
The number of bytes each request contains
explain: Parsing and bandwidth scale with *active* traffic. An idle connection does no work, but in thread-per-connection it still owns a whole thread: a stack, a kernel task, and a place in the scheduler. An event loop keeps only a small per-connection record instead.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Event loops in practice: libuv, timers, thread pools
question: A Node service handles 4 slow password hashes (crypto.pbkdf2, about 100 ms each) at the same moment that 4 requests call fs.readFile. With the default pool, what do the file reads experience?
options: They queue behind the hashes on the 4-thread pool, so they finish roughly 100 ms later than they otherwise would
Nothing, file reads use epoll and never touch the pool
They run on the loop thread and block it
Node starts 4 extra threads automatically for file I/O
explain: Both async pbkdf2 and fs calls run on libuv's shared thread pool, which has 4 threads by default. The hashes occupy all 4, so the file reads wait about one hash duration. Raising UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE or moving hashing elsewhere fixes it. Disk files cannot use epoll at all.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Confidence intervals by bootstrapping over queries
question: Two systems' per-query nDCG@10 values correlate at 0.9 across 100 queries. Compared with an unpaired bootstrap, what does a paired bootstrap of the mean difference give?
options: A wider interval, because pairing loses degrees of freedom
The same interval, because the means are identical either way
A much narrower interval, because shared query difficulty cancels in the per-query differences
An interval centered on a different value
explain: The point estimate is the same mean difference either way. With strong correlation, most per-query variation is query difficulty that hits both systems alike. Differencing per query removes it, so the variance of the difference is much smaller than the sum of the two variances.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Non-executable memory: the NX bit, DEP and W^X
question: A JIT engine maps one page as readable, writable and executable and keeps writing new code into it while it runs. Which policy does this violate, and why does it matter?
options: W^X, because any memory-write bug could place attacker code in a page that is also executable
ASLR, because the page has a fixed address
RELRO, because the page is writable
None: JIT pages are exempt by design
explain: W^X says a page is never writable and executable at the same moment. An always-RWX page gives any write bug a place to put code that will run. The recommended pattern is to write, then switch the page to read and execute only.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Control-flow integrity: checking where indirect calls land
question: Why do most Clang CFI schemes require link-time optimization (-flto)?
options: Because LTO makes the binary smaller
Because the set of valid targets for each indirect call depends on every function in the program, which is only visible when the whole program is linked
Because CFI checks run in the linker at run time
Because LTO disables ASLR
explain: Each call site's allowed set includes all address-taken functions of the right type across all object files. Only at link time, with the whole program visible, can the compiler build those sets and emit tight checks.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Sandboxing as a layer: how Android hardened after Stagefright
question: Android enabled UBSan integer-overflow checks across the media stack. What happens at run time when a crafted file makes `size + chunk_size` overflow?
options: The sum silently wraps and the copy overflows, as before
The check detects the overflow and the process aborts, turning a heap overflow into a crash
The compiler rejects the file
The value is clamped to SIZE_MAX and parsing continues
explain: The sanitizer inserts a check after the addition; on overflow it aborts. Abort is a denial of service at worst, while the unchecked version led to heap corruption and possible code execution.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Why a write steals the whole line: MESI and ownership
question: Core 0 holds line L in Exclusive state and writes to it. What must happen first?
options: Nothing: Exclusive means no other copy exists, so the line silently becomes Modified
An RFO is broadcast to invalidate other copies
The line is written back to main memory
Core 0 must first move the line to Shared
explain: That is the whole point of the Exclusive state: Drepper notes a local write in E does not have to be announced, and that E to M is much faster than S to M. Trouble starts only once another core also wants the line.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: The setting: data that is not allowed to leave the device
question: In cross-device federated learning, which expectation is realistic for a single round?
options: Every device in the population contributes once per round
The same few hundred devices are reused every round so they can carry state
A few hundred devices are chosen from the much larger set currently available, and some of them will not report back
Devices are addressed by identifier so the server can retry a specific one
explain: Availability is the constraint. Tens of thousands of devices may be checking in, the server picks a few hundred, clients are not individually addressable and are treated as stateless, and 5 percent or more of a round's participants are expected to drop out. Carrying per-client state across rounds is a cross-silo luxury.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Non-IID data and client drift: fast convergence to the wrong answer
